title: Longest Joint Run on Spare Batteries
statement:
You have n laptops and a pile of batteries; battery i holds batteries[i] minutes of charge. Each laptop runs on one battery at a time. At the start of any whole minute you may take a battery out of one laptop and put any other battery in, as often as you like, instantly. Batteries never recharge, and one battery cannot power two laptops in the same minute.

Return the largest number of whole minutes during which all n laptops run at the same time.

examples.why: The big battery can only power one laptop per minute. The other laptop gets the two 1-minute batteries. 12 / 2 = 6 is not reachable.
Total charge 9, and no battery is too big to share, so ⌊9 / 2⌋ = 4 minutes.
A single laptop simply uses every battery one after another.

hints: Guess an answer T. How would you check whether all n laptops can run for T minutes?
A battery bigger than T can only ever contribute T minutes, since it cannot power two laptops at once. A smaller one can contribute all of its charge.
T is feasible exactly when the sum of min(battery, T) is at least n · T. That test is monotone in T, so binary search it.

explain.intuition:
If you aim for T minutes, a battery with more than T minutes is wasted beyond T: in any minute it sits in one laptop, so over T minutes it can give at most T. Every battery with T or less can be spread around freely, filling gaps wherever needed. So the usable charge is Σ min(b, T), and the laptops need n · T.

That condition is also enough: line up the capped batteries end to end and cut the line into n strips of length T. A battery split between two strips never overlaps itself in time because it is at most T long. If T works, every smaller T works too, so binary search for the largest feasible T.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = ⌊sum / n⌋, which no answer can exceed.
Take mid = ⌈(lo + hi) / 2⌉ and compute Σ min(b, mid).
If that is at least n · mid, set lo = mid; otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Returning ⌊sum / n⌋ without capping big batteries, as in the first example.
Overflow in languages with 32-bit ints: the sum can reach 10¹⁴. JavaScript numbers are exact up to 2⁵³, which is enough here.
Rounding mid down with lo = mid, which loops forever when hi = lo + 1.

solutions.title: Binary search on the minutes
solutions.idea: T is feasible when the batteries, each capped at T, hold at least n · T minutes in total.

solutions.title: Give oversized batteries their own laptop
solutions.idea: Sort descending. While the largest battery exceeds the average share, dedicate it to one laptop and drop both. The rest is shared evenly.

followups: Swaps may happen at any real moment, not only whole minutes. Does the answer change?
Each laptop has a different power draw. How would the feasibility test change?
